findings_fixed_this_round: BLOCKING, claim integrity: 'TypeScript 7's Go port is 2MB.' Measured 2026-09-04, typescript@7.0.2 — now npm's `latest`, so this is what a reader gets today, not a future scenario — installs 30.7MB: a 3.6MB JavaScript shim plus a 26.5MB platform-native Go binary it cannot run without. The compiler did not shrink by 12x, it grew. The article's conclusion is unchanged and better supported, which is why this is a correction rather than a retraction.

BLOCKING, REVIEW.md pass 3: the install snippet was a single npm line. Now four package managers, the eslint peer range covering 8, 9 and 10, an explicit statement that every other peer is optional, and `npm ls typescript` as the reader's own verification — which is the article's thesis turned into a command.

framing lock: 'Two wins, two axes' tripped sdlc-chain-lock's banned-vocabulary set. This is a genuine false positive — 'wins' here means 'improvements', and the article's own singular 'a size win only' two paragraphs later is not on the list. Reworded to 'Two gains' rather than loosening the gate: the word list is a blunt instrument on purpose, and widening it to admit a benign use would weaken a check that exists to stop competitive framing. Recorded so the inconsistency is visible if it recurs.
checked_and_found_correct: The two-door mechanism, which is the article's spine: @typescript-eslint/utils@8.0.0 declares only an eslint peer, 8.46.2 declares eslint AND typescript, and its peerDependenciesMeta is empty — so that peer is genuinely non-optional. The drift happened after 8.0.0 and was present by 8.20.0.
TypeScript 6.0.3 installs 24,116 KB. The headline 24MB is exact.
oxc-resolver installs 1,632 KB against a claimed 1.5MB, and the utils subtree 4,016 KB against a claimed 4.5MB — both the right instrument, with ordinary version drift.
The devkit's published manifest matches the article's 'Now' block verbatim, and has no `dependencies` field at all, so 'zero runtime dependencies' is literally true.
19 plugins, counted from the monorepo's eslint-plugin-* packages.

growth_hook.why: The hook is a confession with a number in it, which is the most durable kind: a peer the author forgot to mark optional put 24MB under every plugin they publish. The structure keeps paying that off — two theories, both half right, which is why the first fix failed. The closing line does the CTA's job better than a CTA would: '`npm ls typescript` in a project that only installs a linter is an uncomfortable command to run.'

security_correctness.why: Read as technical correctness. The mechanism claims are exact and were verified at the registry rather than from memory, including the subtle one — that the second door is non-optional, which is what makes it independent of the first. The size figures use install-tree measurement consistently, which is the correct instrument and one the article never states; the spec now does. Held here rather than higher because the TypeScript 7 figure was wrong by an order of magnitude in the wrong direction, in an article whose entire subject is size.

structure_framing_voice.why: The strongest lens. 'Two numbers, and they are not the same number' is the section most size articles never write, and it pre-empts exactly the conflation the author says they nearly published. 'The part I got wrong' and 'What is still on the floor' are both unusual and both earn their place — an article that reports a 49% remaining inefficiency and an unshipped -70ms win is not selling anything. 'Nobody reviews a manifest the way they review a function' is the line the piece turns on. Framing is careful: @typescript-eslint/utils is described factually, with the version where the peer appeared, and the author's own manifest is treated as the worse mistake.

compatibility.why: Was a single npm line, which pass 3 blocks. Now carries all four package managers and the peer range across ESLint 8, 9 and 10 — and, unusually, the compatibility section is on-topic rather than boilerplate, because the thing worth saying about installing this package is that it does not drag anything with it. The `npm ls typescript` check gives the reader a way to prove that themselves.

reproducibility.why: The lowest, and the honest reason is that this article contains two classes of number. The install-tree and manifest rows were all re-run on the reviewed date with a stated instrument. The timing figures, the 20-package tarball census, the 49% and the -70ms are dated single-machine measurements at a pinned commit that the article does not name, so a reader cannot re-run them at all. The article does flag them as pinned-commit timings; the spec now records explicitly that they were not re-verified, rather than letting a fully-sourced table imply that everything in it was.
